newsitem.title: USA: McVeigh's lawyers seek delay in bombing trial.
newsitem.headline: McVeigh's lawyers seek delay in bombing trial.

text.p: Oklahoma City bombing suspect Timothy McVeigh asked a federal appeals court to delay Monday's start of his trial, saying pre-trial publicity would prevent a fair hearing.

In documents made public on Friday, McVeigh's lawyers said the appeals courts' intervention was needed because the trial judge was fixated on starting the trial on schedule, "come hell or high water."

"Absent intervention by this court, Mr. McVeigh will be thrust into a trial for his life under fundamentally unfair circumstances which will almost certainly form the basis for a successful appeal," the defence team wrote.
McVeigh could receive the death penalty if convicted of bombing the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995. The attack killed 168 people.

McVeigh's attorneys told the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals that purported confessions by their client, published recently in the Dallas Morning News and Playboy Magazine, were circulated nationally as well as in the Denver area.
McVeigh's attorneys said the articles made it impossible for an impartial jury to be selected.

"The effects of the pre-trial publicity, particularly concerning the alleged confessions, doubtless will have a psychological impact upon jurors who inevitably will conclude 'he confessed, therefore he must be guilty,'" McVeigh's lawyers wrote.
U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch denied McVeigh's request to delay the trial for one year soon after the purported confessions were published.
The request was the third attempt this week by McVeigh's attorneys to delay the start of the trial, scheduled to begin in Denver on Monday.

On Tuesday, McVeigh's lawyers asked the appeals court to delay the trial until it determines whether prosecutors must provide the defence with classified intelligence data from the Central Intelligence Agency and the National Security Agency, among others.
The defence said it needed the material to investigate its theory that a foreign government, possibly Iraq, planned the bombing.

On Wednesday, McVeigh's lawyers again asked the appeals court to delay the trial until they can challenge a law that allows victims to view the trial and testify during the penalty phase if McVeigh is convicted.
